hero.name: Joseph
hero.who: a 52-year-old newspaper sub-editor in Kochi who can no longer read long pieces

story.b: Joseph has edited newspaper copy in Kochi for twenty-six years. At home, a Malayalam novel his daughter gave him at Onam sits on the shelf with a bookmark on page eleven. It has been there since August. Every time he opens it, his hand drifts to his phone within two pages. At work he now reads reporters' stories by skimming the first lines and the quotes. Last week he missed a wrong figure buried in the sixth paragraph, and a correction ran the next morning. On the ferry home to Vypin, he scrolls the whole way instead of watching the backwaters. He used to read whole books on that ferry. He wonders when it changed, and whether something in his head changed too.

ask.q: Joseph cannot get past two pages of a novel anymore. What should he do first?
o: Accept that he is simply getting old
Notice how his daily screen habits might be shaping the way he reads
Buy a fancy e-reader so reading feels exciting again
ask.why: Blaming age skips the real question, and a new gadget brings the same habits along. Joseph spends most of his day skimming, clicking and switching. Noticing how those habits may be training his mind is the first step toward choosing different ones.

chapters.take: When reading feels hard, look at how you spend the rest of your day.

story.b: On Monday, Joseph keeps a pencil tally on a scrap of newsprint for one hour at his desk. Every time he skims instead of reads, he makes a mark. Every time he jumps to another window, another mark. By eleven the scrap is covered. Thirty-four marks, and not one story read from start to end. He looks at his desk: two screens, the newsroom chat, his phone face up beside the tea glass. Twenty-six years ago he edited on paper with a red pen and read every line, because there was nothing else to do. The paper did not try to make him patient. But it trained him, just as these screens are training him now. At lunch, the IT team announces a new alerts app.

ask.q: The new app can ping Joseph for every single update, all day. How should he think about it?
o: The tool will shape how he works and thinks, so he should set it up with care
It hardly matters, since a tool is just a tool
He should turn on every alert so he never misses anything
ask.why: Tools are never neutral. A ping for every update trains Joseph to jump and scan all day, the very habit that is hurting his reading. Calling it just a tool ignores that effect, and every alert makes it worse. Setting it up carefully keeps the tool working for him.

chapters.take: The tools you use every day quietly train the way you think.

story.b: If years of screens could teach his mind to skim, Joseph reasons, then practice might teach it to read again. He makes a rule. Every evening he reads one long feature article from beginning to end, with no other tab open. The first night he gets restless by the fourth paragraph and reaches for his phone twice. The second night is no better. On the fifth night he reaches the end and realises he followed the whole argument. By the second week, reading feels a little less like pushing a stalled scooter uphill. At the office, his colleague Thomas laughs when he hears about it. Thomas says that at their age the brain is like dried coconut, set and finished.

ask.q: Thomas tells Joseph that at fifty-two his brain is too set to change. What should Joseph do?
o: Believe him and go back to skimming
Wait for a long holiday to fix his reading all at once
Keep reading one full article a day, since the mind changes with use
ask.why: The mind keeps adapting to what we practise, which is likely how skimming got so strong in the first place. Believing it is too late wastes that same flexibility. A holiday ends and old habits return. A daily article trains steady reading back, a little at a time.

chapters.take: Whatever you practise grows stronger, including the habit of paying attention.

story.b: On Thursday, Joseph zips his phone into the inside pocket of his bag before the ferry leaves the jetty. He opens the novel at page eleven. The first few minutes are uncomfortable, like sitting in a waiting room with nothing to hold. Then something shifts. The story is set in a village by the backwaters, and he starts picturing his grandmother's house in Alappuzha, the smell of wet earth and coconut oil. He makes connections the writer never wrote. Ten pages pass before the ferry bumps the jetty. That night his daughter Merin calls from Bengaluru. She says the novel is also available as an e-book, full of handy links and notes. It would be easier to carry on his phone, she says.

ask.q: Merin suggests Joseph read the novel on his phone instead, since it is handier. What should he do?
o: Switch to the phone, since reading is reading
Stick with the paper book and keep his phone away while he reads
Read on the phone and tap every link to learn more
ask.why: Deep reading is a skill that needs quiet. On the phone, every notification and link is a small decision that pulls Joseph's attention away. Tapping every link breaks the flow even more. The paper book, with the phone tucked away, gives his mind room to imagine and connect.

chapters.take: Quiet, unbroken reading is a skill, and it needs a quiet place to grow.

story.b: A trainee named Anjali joins the desk. She is quick and clever, and she bookmarks everything: the style guide, spelling lists, a page on how to write dates. When she is unsure, she searches. Joseph realises he does the same now. Years ago he knew the spelling of every town in the district and most style rules by heart. He would read a page and the errors would jump out, because the rules were already inside his head, linked to each other. Now he checks everything and still misses things. On Friday, Anjali sends a page with three errors, all from rules she had bookmarked. She looks embarrassed and asks Joseph how he used to catch them so fast.

ask.q: Anjali asks how she can catch errors faster. What should Joseph advise?
o: Learn the most common rules by heart, so she can spot errors without searching
Keep bookmarking, since everything is online anyway
Print all the rules and stick them beside her screen
ask.why: What lives only in bookmarks cannot connect with anything else in her head. A printout is still storage outside her mind. When Anjali knows the common rules by heart, she can spot patterns and errors at a glance, which is exactly what a good sub-editor needs.

chapters.take: What you truly remember, you can connect. What you only bookmark, you cannot.

story.b: The Sunday editor asks Joseph for a column on how the Fort Kochi waterfront has changed. He has always wanted to write it. He sits at his desk and opens tabs: old photographs, ferry timetables, tourism reports, a dozen blogs. By evening he has twenty tabs open and no idea what he actually wants to say. Everything is fast and useful, and none of it is his own. His head feels full and empty at the same time. The deadline is Thursday. He thinks about opening a few more tabs to find a better angle. Instead, he notices the low sun outside the window and remembers how he used to think best walking by the water.

ask.q: Joseph's column is due and he has twenty open tabs but no angle. What should he try?
o: Open more tabs and gather facts even faster
Borrow the angle of a popular article online
Step away from the screen for some quiet time and let ideas form
ask.why: Gathering facts quickly is useful, but an angle needs slow thinking, and twenty tabs leave no room for it. More tabs just add noise, and a borrowed angle is not his own voice. Quiet time away from screens gives Joseph's mind space to connect what he already knows.

chapters.take: Fast is great for facts. Slow is where your best ideas usually show up.

story.b: Joseph finished the Onam novel in November and is halfway through another. On the ferry to Vypin, his phone stays in his bag and the backwaters are back. He still uses screens all day at work, but he reads every story to the last paragraph, and he has not missed a buried figure since. The waterfront column ran on a Sunday, written after a slow walk along the jetty with a glass of chai. Two readers sent letters about their own memories of the old boat yards. Anjali now knows most of the style guide by heart and catches errors before he does. The scrap of newsprint with thirty-four marks is pinned above his desk, as a reminder.

chapters.take: Your attention goes where you train it. Train it toward depth.
